# Architecture Data, Knowledge, and Representation {#sec-data-representations-world-models}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world."*
>
> — Ludwig Wittgenstein, *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* (1922) [@Wittgenstein1922Tractatus]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Ludwig Wittgenstein argued that language constrains what we
can conceive. The architecture claim is narrower. A method can change only the
design state exposed to it. If a representation has no way to express a
coherence assumption, software dependency, or physical limit, the method
cannot preserve it deliberately.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What must be known, kept current, and made changeable for a method to work on
the real architecture problem?
:::

@sec-architecture-20-ontology ended with a bounded study, not with a method.
The study asks which, if either, of the 3\ MB and 4\ MB L2 candidates should
advance to RTL evaluation against the current 2\ MB baseline for the declared
XR workload. It fixes the workload, software, cache policy, memory system, and
physical limits.
It permits only the L2 capacity to change. Before any method can help, those
facts have to exist in a form that the method can inspect without silently
changing their meaning.

That requirement is easy to underestimate. Model parameters may encode the
RISC-V specification, common cache organizations, and the usual relationships
among capacity, misses, area, latency, and power. None of that knowledge identifies
the current design revision, the software image that will run on it, the
workload snapshot used for comparison, or the conditions under which earlier
results remain relevant. General knowledge can suggest plausible work. It
cannot substitute for the state of this project.

Representation is therefore an architecture decision, not a file-format
choice. It decides which system relationships remain visible, which designs
are reachable, which changes count as adjacent, and which effects can disappear
between a high-level proposal and the artifact a tool evaluates. A method
cannot protect a relationship that its input omits. It also cannot distinguish
a current fact from a stale one unless the representation carries identity and
freshness.

This chapter builds the problem that
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization will act on. The output is a
current, inspectable account of the hardware, software, workload, dependencies,
permitted changes, invariants, history, freshness, blind spots, and known
unknowns. It does not choose a method, rank a candidate, or accept a
measurement. Those decisions belong to later chapters.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Distinguish general architecture knowledge, current project state, and
  project history, identify the responsible source for each field, and stop
  when responsible sources disagree.
- Represent hardware, software, workload, physical constraints, and their
  dependencies as one design problem rather than as unrelated files.
- Declare permitted changes and invariants so that an illegal or bundled change
  is visible before execution.
- Explain how an encoding determines reachable designs and the neighborhood a
  later method will see.
- Test whether represented state still describes the artifact it names and
  state what remains missing or unknown.
- Hand a later method an inspectable architecture problem without prescribing
  generation, prediction, or optimization.

:::

## From a Declared Study to a Represented Problem

A study contract states what the project intends to learn. A problem
representation states what the project is actually prepared to let a method
read and change. The two must agree, but they are not the same artifact. The
contract may say that cache capacity is the only permitted change. The
representation must identify the exact field that controls capacity, the legal
values that the memory implementation can realize, and the dependent
configuration and constraint files that must remain consistent with it.

The Lighthouse cache study makes the distinction concrete
(@tbl-represented-problem).

| **Part of the Problem** | **Representation for the Lighthouse Cache Study** |
| --- | --- |
| Study identity and question | Illustrative study `XR-L2-CAP-A`, contract revision `CONTRACT-A`, and current design revision `XR-COMPUTE-A`. The decision is which, if either, of the 3\ MB and 4\ MB candidates should advance to RTL evaluation against the rerun 2\ MB baseline. These identifiers instantiate the study contract in @sec-architecture-20-ontology. |
| Current hardware | Baseline artifact `L2-2M-A` is the checked-in 2\ MB design generated from revision `XR-COMPUTE-A`. The hardware owner is responsible for the configuration, generator revision, generated cache instance, and linked implementation collateral. |
| Fixed hardware and software state | Cache policy `CACHE-POLICY-A`, NoC `NOC-A`, memory-system configuration `MEMSYS-A`, 2\ GHz microarchitecture, compiler `COMPILER-A`, runtime `RUNTIME-A`, and RISC-V software image `SW-BASE-A`. Their responsible hardware or software owner controls each identifier. |
| Workload state | Workload snapshot `XR-TRACE-A`, including stable frame identifiers and boundaries, collection policy, and workload owner. |
| Candidate set and mapping | The field `l2.capacity` admits exactly `2MB`, `3MB`, and `4MB`, which lower to candidate artifacts `L2-2M-A`, `L2-3M-A`, and `L2-4M-A`. The 2\ MB artifact is the rerun baseline. |
| Permitted change | Only `l2.capacity` may change. Cache policy, associativity, NoC topology, compiler, runtime, memory system, and all other architecture choices remain fixed. |
| Constraints and required checks | This study checks modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power at or below 3\ W, cache macro area at or below 1.5\ mm^2^, and modeled access time at or below 2.5\ ns. Thermal and IR-drop reviews remain independent later requirements. |
| Relationships to preserve | Capacity may change miss behavior, which may change the frame-time distribution. It also changes macro organization and may change power, area, access time, and later physical integration. Workload, software, cache policy, and memory-system conditions must remain tied to every comparison. |
| Source identity | Contract `CONTRACT-A`; design `XR-COMPUTE-A`; hardware, software, and workload identifiers above; cycle-level simulator `SIM-A`; cache model `CACHE-A`; power model `PM-A`; SRAM model `SRAM-A`; and process, voltage, and temperature assumptions `PVT-A`. The study record names the owner of each source. |
| History | The initial live history is empty. A prior result enters comparable history only when the contract permits reuse and its design, candidate, hardware, software, workload, simulator, cache, power, SRAM, and PVT identities match. A nonmatching result may remain linked as advisory context but is not an observation for this study. The walkthrough in @sec-architecture-20-ontology is illustrative and is not entered as live history. |
| Freshness checks | Recorded versions or hashes, named owners, timestamps where needed, and a successful regeneration or consistency check between represented state and the checked-in artifact. |
| Blind spots | No detailed floorplan or congestion result, no completed thermal or IR-drop review, incomplete workload coverage beyond `XR-TRACE-A`, and any hardware effect not modeled by the declared tools. |
| Known unknowns | Whether either larger cache improves 99th-percentile frame time enough to advance, and whether later physical review will uncover an effect absent from the current representation. |
| Study boundary | Four cycle-level executions including infrastructure reruns, one SRAM evaluation per capacity, and a decision to recommend at most one candidate for later RTL study. No implementation or product commitment is authorized. |
| Exclusions and useful scope | Cache-policy, prefetching, coherence, NoC, compiler, software-scheduling, floorplanning, thermal-signoff, IR-drop-signoff, security, reliability, and product-cost changes are excluded. The representation supports only the declared cache-capacity comparison, not a complete model of the XR subsystem or product. |

: **The represented problem makes the declared study inspectable.** It connects
the current design, workload, legal changes, dependencies, history, freshness,
and limits without selecting a method or claiming a result.
{#tbl-represented-problem tbl-colwidths="[24,66]"}

This table is not a demand for one monolithic database. The fields may live in
a configuration schema, workload manifest, version-control record, candidate
table, and run directory. What matters is shared identity. Every artifact must
refer to the same study, design version, workload version, and candidate. A
directory full of individually valid files is not a represented problem if no
one can tell which files describe the same comparison.

The table also prevents scope from expanding unnoticed. Nothing in the
declared study permits changes to issue width, reorder-buffer depth, MAC array
dimensions, the compiler, or the NoC. A method that proposes any of them has
not found a more creative cache design. It has left the study.

## What the Project Knows and Which Source Controls

Architecture work draws on three kinds of knowledge. Each answers a different
question.

General architecture knowledge contains slow-moving relationships,
specifications, common mechanisms, and lessons from prior designs. It can
explain why cache capacity may affect misses or why a clock-domain crossing
needs synchronization. Model parameters, papers, manuals, and design guidance
can all carry this knowledge.

Current project state names the design that exists now. It includes the
active hardware and software versions, workload, mutable fields, constraints,
assumptions, and unresolved conditions. This state changes with the project and
must be explicit.

Project history records what this project tried, what the tools returned,
what failed, what reviewers rejected, and why. It prevents a current design
from being separated from the work that produced it.

A method often needs all three. They must remain distinct because they have
different authority and rates of change. A paper can explain an architectural
relationship but cannot override the checked-in design. A retrieved manual can
clarify a tool option but cannot establish which option the current run used.
An old run can reveal a risk but cannot automatically stand in for a current
measurement.

### Sources Are Not Interchangeable

Papers, specifications, source code, RTL, traces, tool reports, failed
candidates, review notes, and field observations preserve different
relationships. The relevant distinction is not text versus numbers. It is
which question a source can answer, which context it omits, and how a reader
can connect it to the current design (@tbl-dataset-capability).

| **Source Structure** | **What It Can Preserve** | **What It Cannot Establish Alone** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paper, manual, or specification | Concepts, requirements, interfaces, prior findings, and source-linked rationale. | The current project version or whether a local implementation satisfies the requirement. |
| Question and answer or design note | Focused reasoning, calculations, and review rationale. | Executable state, complete dependencies, or conditions not written into the note. |
| Code, RTL, configuration, or typed intermediate representation | Concrete structure, parameter values, interfaces, and buildable state within the properties the format expresses. | Workload coverage, design intent, or physical effects that require later tools. |
| Workload trace or profile | Observed software behavior under a stated capture or sampling policy. | Behavior outside the captured population or effects the collection method cannot observe. |
| Tool run and report | An observation under a particular design, tool, configuration, seed, model, and workload. | A general rule beyond those conditions. |
| Rejected candidate or review decision | A boundary that mattered, the conditions that exposed it, and the reason work stopped. | Whether the same rejection still applies after the design or conditions change. |

: **Source structure determines what can be carried into later work.** More
data does not repair a missing relationship, version, or condition.
{#tbl-dataset-capability tbl-colwidths="[24,36,30]"}

This is one reason architecture data differs from a conventional image
classification dataset. A label such as *cat* can be useful without a build
manifest. A cycle count, power estimate, or timing failure is uninterpretable
without the design, workload, tool path, and assumptions that produced it.
Hardware also has hard structural boundaries. One wrong connection can make a
design unusable, and tightly coupled changes can move performance, power,
timing, area, and software behavior together. A large corpus of disconnected
artifacts does not recover those relationships.

Public benchmarks add another risk. Models trained on public HDL corpora may
have seen the standard benchmark solutions, and contamination studies have
found this pattern in common Verilog benchmarks [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated].
The same concern appears in broader language-model evaluation
[@Balloccu2024Leakage]. A benchmark score cannot establish general design
ability when the evaluated artifacts may have appeared in training. Held-out
designs, source identity, and executable checks matter more than the volume of
examples.

Successful designs can also present a biased view of the space. When a project
retains the winning configuration while deleting failed synthesis runs,
unroutable netlists, and rejected alternatives, the remaining data is not an
unbiased sample. The missing records are concentrated near the boundaries that
later work most needs to understand. A timing failure may report only that
slack became negative, and a crashed run may return no metric at all. Treating
the surviving results as though they were an unbiased sample makes the feasible
region look larger than it is.[^fn-censored-c04]

[^fn-censored-c04]: **Censored observation.** The result says that a value lies
beyond a threshold without measuring the value itself. A timing violation, for
example, may establish that a frequency target was not met without identifying
the highest frequency the design could sustain.

### Different Sources Carry Different Costs and Limits

The same design may be examined with an analytical model, trace replay,
cycle-level simulator, RTL simulation, FPGA platform, or fabricated silicon.
These sources differ in cost, speed, abstraction, and observability
(@fig-data-fidelity-pyramid, @tbl-synthetic-data-costs). They do not form one
fidelity ranking for every property. Gate-level analysis may preserve target
timing detail that an FPGA mapping does not, while an FPGA platform may execute
far more workload than that analysis can cover. Silicon can reveal behavior of
the fabricated design but cannot recover a counterfactual configuration that
was never built.

![**Architecture observations come from sources with different costs and
property coverage.** The arrangement shows a common path from abstract
estimation to a fabricated instance, not a total fidelity order. No source
answers every architecture question.](images/F4-data-pyramid){#fig-data-fidelity-pyramid
fig-alt="Six observation sources arranged from analytical models through
trace-driven, cycle-level, RTL and gate-level analysis, FPGA or emulation, and
physical silicon. The diagram states that the sources have different
properties and costs rather than one universal fidelity order." width="100%"}

| **Source** | **Useful For** | **Important Limit to Represent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical model | Fast sensitivity studies and early bounds. | Simplifying equations, calibration range, and omitted interactions. |
| Trace-driven model | Repeatable study of behavior contained in a captured instruction or event stream. | No behavior that depends on timing feedback absent from the trace. |
| Cycle-level simulator | Detailed modeled microarchitectural behavior. | Simulator abstractions, unsupported states, calibration, and execution cost. |
| RTL or gate-level flow | Logic behavior and implementation-facing checks within the executed flow. | Test coverage, process assumptions, constraint quality, and physical effects outside the flow. |
| FPGA or emulation platform | High-throughput functional or timing-model execution after mapping. | Mapping differences, compile cost, debug visibility, and non-transferable ASIC power or timing. |
| Fabricated silicon | Behavior of a physical implementation under measured conditions. | Limited design variants, observability, stepping, test conditions, and inability to answer every counterfactual question. |

: **Every observation source has a useful scope and a blind spot.** The
representation records both so that later chapters can choose and evaluate a
tool path for the actual question.
{#tbl-synthetic-data-costs tbl-colwidths="[20,34,36]"}

Planned method cost belongs to
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. Realized tool cost and
movement among observation sources belong to
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, while measurement
interpretation belongs to @sec-feedback-verification-trust. This chapter needs
only the representation consequence. A stored observation must name enough of
its source conditions for a later architect to decide whether it applies.

### Knowledge Objects Need Field-Specific Authority

Knowledge also differs by where it lives (@tbl-knowledge-objects). Collapsing
all of these objects into the word *memory* or *context* hides their different
roles.

| **Object** | **What It Preserves** | **Authority and Freshness Rule** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model parameters | Learned statistical regularities and general concepts. | Useful as prior knowledge, never the authoritative record of current project state. |
| Retrieval index and retrieved material | Source-linked manuals, papers, examples, and project documents selected for the current task. | Authority belongs to the underlying source. Version and date must match the use. |
| In-context working set | Instructions, selected sources, current state, and examples needed for one operation. | Transient assembly only. It does not become project state unless an authorized update records it. |
| Study contract | Question, comparator, scope, permitted changes, constraints, measurements, budget, and stopping conditions. | Controls the declared comparison until an authorized revision changes the contract. |
| Explicit design and software state | Current configuration, generated artifacts, software image, manifests, and linked constraints. | Current only when the designated sources agree and consistency checks pass. |
| Workload state | Trace, profile, population, phase definitions, sampling policy, and version. | Controls the workload condition only within its recorded coverage. |
| Project history | Prior candidates, tool runs, failures, decisions, and rationale linked to their conditions. | Authoritative for what was recorded then, not automatically applicable to the current version. |

: **Knowledge objects preserve different facts.** Authority belongs to the
source responsible for a field, not to whichever object was supplied most
recently.
{#tbl-knowledge-objects tbl-colwidths="[23,38,29]"}

There is no safe global rule that one file always wins. The study contract
controls the permitted comparison. The checked-in configuration and generated
artifact control implemented hardware state when they agree. The workload
manifest controls which trace is current. The specification controls an
interface requirement. A review decision controls whether a candidate
advanced. When responsible sources disagree, the conflict is not silently
resolved in favor of the most convenient one. The study blocks until the owner
reconciles the mismatch or records an authorized change.

Knowledge enters these objects on different schedules. General relationships
may be learned during model training. Manuals and prior reports may be
retrieved when needed. Current constraints belong in explicit project state,
not in model weights. Tool results append to project history only after their
identity and conditions are known. The durable update-path rule is simple
(@tbl-ingestion-timescales). Fast-changing facts need an explicit, versioned
path. Slow-changing knowledge can inform work but cannot override those facts.

| **Knowledge Path** | **Appropriate Content** | **Required Check Before Use** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model training or adaptation | General architecture concepts, recurring relationships, and interaction conventions. | Treat as prior knowledge and verify against responsible project sources. |
| Retrieval from a source collection | Manuals, specifications, prior studies, and versioned internal documents. | Confirm source identity, revision, and applicability. |
| Current working context | The subset of contract, state, history, and sources needed for the immediate task. | Confirm that it was assembled from current responsible sources. |
| Authorized project update | A new contract revision, design state, workload, constraint, decision, or accepted record. | Record owner, version, dependencies, and consistency checks. |

: **The update path should match how quickly a fact changes.** Current project
facts require explicit versioned updates. General knowledge remains advisory.
{#tbl-ingestion-timescales tbl-colwidths="[24,38,28]"}

## Representation Determines Reachable Designs

A project can have the right facts and still represent them badly. The encoding
decides which designs can be expressed, which dependencies remain connected,
and which changes a later method will regard as nearby. These are architecture
consequences.

### Structure, Text, and Tool-Facing Forms

Raw text is useful for explanation but weak as the sole representation of a
design. It can describe an L2 change without identifying the configuration
field, affected interfaces, or companion constraints. Tool-facing
representations add structure. Parameter schemas enumerate legal values.
Abstract syntax trees and data-flow graphs preserve relationships that a token
sequence makes difficult to inspect. Typed intermediate representations can
reject malformed constructions before expensive execution. Parameterized
generators can expose a bounded set of changes while retaining the lowering
path to RTL.

Typed representations are not safe in general. They reject only violations
covered by their types and checks. SystemVerilog, FIRRTL, typed dialects in the
CIRCT compiler infrastructure, and companion formats such as SDC and UPF
preserve different properties [@CIRCT] (@tbl-representation-formats).

| **Representation** | **What It Makes Explicit** | **What Still Requires Attention** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SystemVerilog or VHDL | Logic, hierarchy, interfaces, and behavior in the HDL. | Width conventions, connectivity, unknown values, verification intent, and all properties not established by compilation. |
| Typed hardware IR such as FIRRTL or a CIRCT dialect | Operations, types, connectivity, and transformations supported by the IR. | Legal designs the IR cannot express, semantic correctness, lowering, verification, and physical realization. |
| Parameter schema and generator | Named mutable fields, legal values, and a reproducible path to generated artifacts. | Whether the generator and checked-in artifacts agree and whether dependent collateral changes with the design. |
| SDC, UPF, and other constraint collateral | Timing, power intent, domains, path references, and implementation assumptions. | Hierarchical-name coupling, stale paths, waived checks, and consistency with the RTL. |
| Graph or spatial representation | Connectivity, topology, adjacency, or physical location. | Features omitted from nodes and edges, write-back to tool inputs, and physical rules not encoded in the graph. |

: **A representation makes some properties explicit and leaves others for
later checks.** Choosing one also chooses which legal designs are easy,
difficult, or impossible to express.
{#tbl-representation-formats tbl-colwidths="[24,34,32]"}

::: {.callout-field-note title="The missing level shifter"}
A text-based proposal connects logic across two voltage domains without a level
shifter. The code passes syntax checks, but the represented design omitted the
power-domain relationship that made the connection illegal. This composite
example captures the real lesson. Better prose would not fix the problem. The
design state must carry the domains and the required crossing rule in a form
the tool path can check.
:::

Hardware is concurrent and relational. A netlist is a graph, a memory hierarchy
is a topology, and a floorplan adds spatial coordinates. Graph encodings can
preserve fan-in, fan-out, connectivity, and structural locality more directly
than a one-dimensional token stream. DeepGate2, for example, learns over
and-inverter graphs rather than treating a circuit only as text
[@ShiEtAl2023DeepGate2]. A graph still omits any property not attached to its
nodes, edges, or surrounding state. Logical adjacency is not physical
proximity, and a graph without placement cannot establish wire delay.

The macro-placement work associated with AlphaChip provides a useful
representation example. The chip was represented with graph structure for
connectivity and a grid-like canvas for legal placement. Those choices exposed
relationships and spatial actions that flat RTL text did not
[@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement]. The result
does not establish that one placement method is generally best. It shows that a
method can search only after the architecture problem has been translated into
a form that preserves the relationships relevant to the task. The policy and
reward loop belong with optimization in
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization rather than in this chapter.

### Workload Is Part of Design State {#sec-workload-phase-behavior}

Static hardware does not identify what it will run. A workload representation
must carry the software image, inputs, trace or profile, phase definitions,
sampling policy, and coverage limits relevant to the study. Those fields are
not background metadata. They determine which hardware behavior becomes
visible.

The Lighthouse XR workload is bursty and phase dependent. A trace can expose
frame boundaries, memory behavior, and periods of activity. It may still omit
timing feedback that would have changed the instruction stream, thread
interleaving, or system behavior. A trace captured under one software image
cannot silently stand in for another. The representation must connect
`XR-TRACE-A` to `SW-BASE-A`, its frame identifiers, its collection policy, and
the hardware conditions under which it is used.

Representative sampling can reduce detailed simulation cost without changing
the simulator itself. SimPoint clusters recurring execution phases and
simulates representative intervals, while SMARTS uses statistical sampling and
reports confidence for the estimate
[@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The durable
representation point is not which sampling scheme to choose. It is that the
selected intervals, weights, and coverage become part of workload state. A
sampled result without those fields cannot be interpreted or reproduced.

### Permitted Changes and Invariants

A representation must separate what may change from what must remain fixed. In
the Lighthouse study, L2 capacity is the only mutable architecture field. The
2\ MB, 3\ MB, and 4\ MB choices must map to realizable cache configurations.
Cache policy, NoC topology, compiler, runtime, software image, workload, and the
rest of the memory system remain fixed. The 3\ W power envelope, 1.5\ mm^2^
macro-area limit, 2.5\ ns access-time allocation, and independent thermal and
IR-drop review remain required.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One permitted change, with its dependencies"}
**The declared move.** Select one realizable L2 capacity from 2\ MB, 3\ MB, and
4\ MB.

**What moves with it.** The capacity field, generated cache instance, and any
derived configuration needed to keep the artifact consistent.

**What does not move.** Cache policy, NoC topology, compiler, runtime, workload,
software image, memory system, and the declared limits and reviews.

**Why the boundary matters.** A proposal that changes capacity and compiler
behavior may be an interesting new study. It is not a valid candidate in this
comparison.
:::

The distinction also separates parametric and structural changes. A parametric
change selects a value within an existing structure, such as a legal cache
capacity or queue depth. A structural change alters the set of components or
relationships, such as adding a pipeline stage, replacing a mesh with a ring,
or inserting an accelerator. Structural changes require a different schema,
different dependent artifacts, and often a different study. Calling both
changes simply *edits* hides the difference.

System and software contracts matter even when they live outside the local
configuration. A new vector instruction affects the ISA, compiler, runtime,
and verification plan, and it may also require control and status register
changes. A memory organization that
improves average latency but violates the memory consistency model is not a
legal system design. Backward compatibility, interface standards, and
software assumptions must appear as dependencies or invariants rather than
remaining with the one experienced engineer who remembers them.

Physical collateral is coupled in the same way. Timing and power-intent files
often refer to exact hierarchical paths. Renaming or moving a block without
updating SDC or UPF can leave a constraint pointing to nothing. A legal change
therefore includes its required companion changes. The representation should
make that group visible so a later method cannot improve one file while
silently invalidating another.

Fixed conditions may also be a set rather than one point. Multi-corner,
multi-mode analysis represents a physical design across operating modes and
process, voltage, and temperature corners. A candidate must retain the same
identity across the declared condition matrix, and each observation must name
the condition it covers. A typical-corner result cannot silently stand in for a
fast-corner hold check or a low-power operating mode.

### Encoding Changes the Geometry

Even a correct list of legal values imposes a geometry on later search. Suppose
cache capacity is encoded on a linear numerical axis. A move from 512\ KB to
1\ MB then appears to be the same distance as a move from 4\ MB to 4.5\ MB.
The architectural effects are unlikely to be comparable, and 4.5\ MB may not
be realizable with the available SRAM macros. The encoding has created a
misleading neighborhood and an impossible point.

Two checks expose the problem. First, compare adjacent steps at different parts
of the encoded range. If equal encoded steps produce very different changes in
the architectural quantity of interest, the distance is misleading. Second,
ask whether every encoded point lowers to a configuration the tools can build.
An index over realizable macro organizations may be better than a continuous
capacity value. A logarithmic capacity axis may better reflect some cache
relationships than a linear one. These are design inferences for this example,
not prescriptions from one modeling paper. More broadly, classical
architecture design-space models use transformations and nonlinear terms when
parameter effects and interactions are not well represented on the original
axes [@LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling].

The lesson does not prescribe an optimizer. It precedes method selection.
Generation, prediction, and optimization all inherit the reachable set and
neighborhood created here. A poor encoding can make any of them waste effort
on impossible candidates or miss useful ones that were never expressible.

## Keeping State Current and Exposing Its Limits

A represented problem changes over time. The configuration moves, a workload
is recaptured, a model is recalibrated, or a constraint changes. Project
history and freshness checks keep those changes from turning into silent
contradictions.

### History Includes Rejected Work

An execution history connects each candidate to the prior state, proposed
change, conditions, tool return, run status, candidate disposition, and design
decision (@fig-execution-history). A completed run may be followed by adoption,
rejection, or an unresolved comparison. An infrastructure failure supports
none of those candidate dispositions and instead calls for repair or rerun.
Only an explicit decision to adopt a change creates a new design version.

![**A versioned execution history separates run status, candidate disposition,
and design change.** A completed execution may be followed by adoption,
rejection, or an unresolved comparison. An infrastructure failure leads to
repair rather than a candidate verdict, and only explicit adoption creates a new design
state.](images/F5a-trajectory-record){#fig-execution-history width="85%"
fig-alt="Project history showing a valid result followed by an explicit
adoption and new state, a valid result that remains rejected or unresolved, and
an infrastructure failure that leads to repair while the design state remains
unchanged."}

The cache walkthrough in @sec-architecture-20-ontology illustrated a
stale-state failure, a rejected 4\ MB candidate, and an unresolved 3\ MB
comparison. This chapter does not import those illustrative outcomes as live
history. The initial live history is empty. A prior result becomes a comparable
observation only when its contract status and recorded design, candidate,
hardware, software, workload, simulator, cache, power, SRAM, and PVT
identifiers satisfy the matching rule in @tbl-represented-problem. Other
records can remain visible as advisory context without becoming observations
for this study.

Projects need negative records because successful designs are survivor
samples. Removing failed work makes both a dataset and an active study
optimistic near the feasibility boundary. The record should preserve why a run
failed without turning one local result into a universal prohibition
(@tbl-negative-traces).

| **Failed Run or Rejected Alternative** | **What to Keep** | **How Later Work Should Use It** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Synthesis or timing violation | Candidate, constraints, process assumptions, and failing paths. | Reconsider the candidate only after checking whether the relevant conditions still apply. |
| Unroutable or power-delivery failure | Netlist, placement conditions, density, congestion, or IR-drop result. | Identify the affected region and avoid treating the failure as a property of all similar designs. |
| Proxy improvement overturned later | Cheap estimate, later observation, and the conditions under which they diverged. | Reassess the proxy's useful scope before reuse. |
| Tool failure or crash | Command, inputs, environment identity, logs, and failure classification. | Repair the environment without recording the candidate as architecturally rejected. |
| Coverage gap | Missing workload, input, scenario, or architecture class. | Mark the boundary of the result rather than filling it with an assumption. |
| Reviewer rejection | Candidate, stated reason, risk, schedule, integration concern, and decision owner. | Preserve the rationale and revisit it only when the relevant conditions change. |
| Waiver or exception | Violated rule, justification, scope, owner, and expiration or review condition. | Prevent repeated work while keeping the exception visible. |

: **Rejected work remains useful when its conditions are recorded.** A later
architect can determine whether the same boundary still applies.
{#tbl-negative-traces tbl-colwidths="[27,34,29]"}

### Freshness Is a Property of the Representation

General knowledge and project state age at different rates. A current
retrieval index can point to an old manual. A current design can be paired with
a trace captured from an earlier software image. A run directory can contain a
new report and an old configuration. Each file may look plausible on its own
while the combination describes no design that ever existed
(@fig-split-brain-causality).

![**A stale source can make a current design appear internally
consistent.** When a method reads an earlier specification or project state, it
can propose a change that violates the version now under
design.](images/F4b-split-brain-causality){#fig-split-brain-causality
width="100%" fig-alt="A stale reference state and a current project state lead
to an incompatible proposal. Version and freshness checks expose the mismatch
before the proposal reaches a costly tool flow."}

The represented state can also drift from the artifact it claims to describe.
A parameter is renamed in the generator, a constraint is tightened directly in
an SDC file, or a block is replaced by hand. The state still says it is current,
but regenerating the design produces something different from the checked-in
artifact.

The direct check is to regenerate the artifact from the represented state and
compare the result with the repository. If the state cannot reproduce the
design it names, work that depends on it should not start. This check has a
clear limit. It works only where the state owns generation. A hand edit below
that level must be detected by another consistency check or made an explicit
part of state.

Source identity needs enough detail to support these checks. Depending on the
artifact, that may mean a version-control revision, content hash, tool and model
version, workload manifest, seed, process corner, timestamp, or named owner.
The representation should keep only what the study needs, but it cannot omit
the identity required to decide whether two records describe the same
conditions.

### Cross-Layer Relationships Need Provenance

Freshness also runs vertically through the stack. A high-level decision such as
adding a prefetcher may be lowered through generators, RTL, synthesis,
placement, and timing analysis. If a later timing failure cannot be connected
back to the architecture construct that produced it, the design state
fragments when the team most needs an explanation.

Cross-layer provenance records those relationships. It connects architecture
intent to the implementation objects and constraints that realize it. It does
not prove that every transformation preserved meaning. It makes the chain
inspectable and can localize a missing link or failed consistency check.
Detecting semantic loss still requires a check for the property that should
have survived.

Common architecture artifacts become reusable only when their hidden context is
made visible (@tbl-representation-debt).

| **Artifact** | **What It Preserves** | **What It Often Hides** | **Resulting Blind Spot** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Paper or plot | Reported claim, result, and comparison. | Tool flags, failed candidates, and tuning history. | The endpoint is visible but the path cannot be reconstructed. |
| Workload trace | Captured input behavior and measurements. | Population, coverage, version, sampling, and privacy filters. | The design may be optimized for an unrepresentative slice. |
| Simulator configuration | Model settings and selected options. | Defaults, unsupported states, calibration limits, and dependent software. | A number may be trusted outside the simulator's useful scope. |
| RTL or EDA report | Implementation-facing structure or feedback. | Process assumptions, constraints, waived warnings, and intent. | A locally valid artifact may not satisfy the system decision. |
| Cross-layer mapping | Links from architecture choices to lower-level objects. | Intermediate transformations not recorded in the mapping. | A physical failure may not be traceable to the choice that caused it. |
| Review note | Judgment, rationale, risk, and decision. | Unstated assumptions or alternatives never entered into the record. | Later work remembers the verdict but not its conditions. |
| Rejected candidate | A boundary and a negative result. | Failure reason, tool path, workload, or design version. | The team either repeats the failure or excludes too much. |

: **Architecture artifacts are reusable only within their recorded context.**
Provenance, assumptions, constraints, and coverage expose what each artifact
does and does not support.
{#tbl-representation-debt tbl-colwidths="[20,28,27,25]"}

### Blind Spots and Known Unknowns Stay Visible

An adequate representation is not one that contains everything. It states what
it contains, what it omits, and the scope within which it remains useful.
Building a complete digital description of a modern system would cost more than
most studies could justify and would still miss something.

Blind spots are omitted or unobserved relationships that could matter. The
Lighthouse cache representation has no detailed floorplan or congestion result,
no completed thermal or IR-drop review, and no guarantee that
`XR-TRACE-A` covers every deployed workload condition. Known unknowns are
questions already recognized but not yet resolved, such as whether a larger
cache improves tail frame time enough to advance.

The distinction matters. A known unknown can be planned for. A blind spot may
surface only after a later tool, reviewer, or field observation exposes it.
Both should remain visible so that a later method does not convert missing
information into an assumed favorable value.

For this bounded study, @tbl-represented-problem is the minimum handoff. It
contains enough identity and context to reconstruct the comparison, expose
legal changes, and recognize when the representation is no longer useful. A
longer-lived or more consequential use needs more retained history and source
identity. The rules for claims that leave the project belong to the ownership
and accountability discussion later in the book.

## The Handoff to Method Choice

@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization needs an inspectable problem,
not a prescribed technique. The Lighthouse handoff therefore contains the
following items.

1. The current design, software, workload, and study identity.
2. The exact legal candidate set and the fields that implement each change.
3. The invariants, constraints, and dependent artifacts that must remain
   consistent.
4. The relationships the study intends to observe.
5. Compatible project history, including rejected work and infrastructure
   failures.
6. Source identity, freshness checks, and conflict-resolution rules.
7. Blind spots, known unknowns, and the useful scope of the representation.

It intentionally contains no proposed next candidate, predicted consequence,
surrogate, optimizer, acceptance threshold for a model, or execution result.
Those additions would answer questions this chapter has not yet asked.
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization can now decide whether the
limiting work calls for conventional analysis, no AI component, generation,
prediction, optimization, or a minimal combination.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces can decide how the chosen work
is connected to tools. @sec-feedback-verification-trust can decide what
feedback means. The order protects the study from being reshaped around the
first available method.

The handoff is inadequate if it cannot reproduce or identify the current
design, if it hides a controlling hardware-software or physical relationship,
if its legal actions bundle undeclared changes, if its sources disagree without
a resolution, or if no one can state where the representation is useful.

## Open Research Questions

**How can AI-assisted methods learn from failed and censored design data without
treating every local failure as a universal boundary?** Failed runs contain
valuable information near feasibility limits, but their meaning depends on the
exact design, tools, workload, and constraints that produced them.

**Which representation lets a method preserve the neighborhood that matters
for a given architecture decision?** A scalar schema, graph, spatial model, or
typed IR makes different relationships visible and creates different notions
of adjacency.

**How can an automated method detect that represented state no longer describes
the artifact it names?** Regeneration catches divergence where state owns the
build, but hand edits, generated collateral, and external tool transformations
create additional paths for drift.

**How should a method represent hardware and software dependencies when no
single artifact owns the interface between them?** ISA, compiler, runtime,
firmware, and microarchitecture changes often cross repositories and
organizational boundaries.

**What is the smallest useful record for an AI-assisted bounded study?** Too
little state makes a result uninterpretable, while indiscriminate capture
creates cost, privacy, and maintenance burdens that can outlive the study.

**How can a method expose a blind spot that no current source has named?**
Declared omissions can be recorded directly, but unrecognized missing
relationships may appear only after a later tool, reviewer, or workload exposes
them.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Representation is an architecture decision"}
A method can preserve only the state, relationships, legal changes, and limits
that its representation makes visible.
:::

A generic model and a folder of design files may help frame an early question,
but they cannot support a project-specific architecture decision without
current state. The work needs that state to connect hardware, software,
workload, constraints, and history to one declared study. General knowledge can
inform the state but cannot replace it. Prior results can warn or guide only
when their conditions remain applicable.

The encoding then determines which designs are reachable and which changes
appear related. Typed IRs, parameter schemas, graphs, spatial forms, workload
records, and physical collateral each preserve some properties and omit
others. The architect's task is not to select the richest possible format. It
is to preserve the relationships that control the current question and expose
the ones that remain missing.

Freshness is part of the same decision. A state that cannot reproduce or
identify the artifact it names is not current. A history without conditions is
not reusable. A result with no workload or tool identity is not an architecture
observation that another study can safely apply.

The chapter's output is the represented problem in
@tbl-represented-problem. It contains the current state, legal changes,
dependencies, history, freshness, blind spots, and known unknowns for the
Lighthouse cache study. It does not determine how to explore that problem.
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization takes the next step by deciding
whether the work needs conventional analysis, no AI component, generation,
prediction, optimization, or a minimal combination.
